processing: Ripe pu-erh made mainly with grade 6 leaf and pressed into a brick, commonly of 250 g.
harvest_season: Not tied to one picking: it is a blend of fermented material.
appearance_dry: A 250 g dark brown brick of mid-grade leaf; some bricks of this recipe were sold without an original wrapper.
appearance_liquor: Dark red-brown, as usual for Menghai ripe pu-erh.
appearance_wet: Soft mid-sized dark brown leaf, as usual for a grade 6 blend.
taste_profile: Well regarded among Menghai ripe teas, though detailed notes are few; expect earth, wood and dark sweetness, smoothing out with age.

brewing.notes: Bricks are often tight, so lift flakes along the layers with a pick. Rinse once and use near-boiling water.

vintage_note: Sold by production year, and aged examples such as 2002 Menghai bricks still circulate. Check whether a brick is really from Menghai: a 7562 recipe brick from 2000 is sold by one retailer as a small-batch imitation of the Dayi recipe rather than a factory tea. Unwrapped old bricks deserve extra caution.
description:
7562 is the Menghai Tea Factory's ripe brick recipe, a 250 g format that gives you the factory's ripe style without a big cake. It is also a reference point: the 0562 cake is described in terms of it.

A Japanese account of the tea says it mainly uses grade 6 leaf, which fits an informal reading of the number in which the third digit gives the main grade. As with any ripe tea, the leaf is piled and fermented before pressing.

Expect the usual Menghai ripe cup of earth, wood and a dark sweetness, and more smoothness in older bricks. Flake it carefully along the layers, rinse once, and keep the water very hot.

The buying trap is the phrase 7562 recipe. It can mean a tea made by someone else in imitation, as with one small-batch 2000 brick on the market, so it is not the same as a factory brick. Ask who pressed it and how you can tell.
history:
Little is documented about the origin of 7562 in factory records. On the informal reading of Menghai numbers it would date to 1975, but no official confirmation of that is available. The Menghai Tea Factory was state-run until it became fully private in 1996 and adopted the Dayi mark.

The recipe was popular enough to be imitated: at least one retailer sells a 2000 small-batch brick made in its image from blended Menghai ripe tea, alongside genuine 2002 Menghai bricks.
